title: Postgres MVCC: Tuple Versions, Vacuum, and Wraparound
summary: A deep field guide to how PostgreSQL implements multi-version concurrency control — row version headers, xmin/xmax visibility rules, snapshots, dead tuple accumulation, HOT updates, autovacuum tuning, and transaction ID wraparound. Covers the internals, the practical monitoring queries, the trade-offs versus undo-log engines, and the mistakes that bloat or freeze a production database.

chapters.title: Why MVCC Exists
points: MVCC = Multi-Version Concurrency Control: readers see a consistent snapshot without blocking writers
Core rule in Postgres: readers never block writers, writers never block readers
An UPDATE does not overwrite a row in place; it writes a NEW row version and marks the old one expired
A DELETE does not erase bytes; it only stamps the existing version as expired
Every row version is called a 'tuple'; a logical row is a chain of tuple versions over time
Alternative to MVCC: two-phase locking, where a reader takes a shared lock and stalls writers — Postgres avoids this
Alternative implementation: undo logs (Oracle, MySQL InnoDB) keep one current row plus a rollback segment
Postgres chose in-heap versioning: old versions live in the same table pages as live rows
Consequence 1: rollback is nearly free — just mark the transaction aborted, no undo replay
Consequence 2: cleanup is not free — dead tuples must be reclaimed later by VACUUM
This is the single trade-off that explains bloat, autovacuum, and wraparound as one connected story
MVCC gives snapshot isolation by default at READ COMMITTED, which is Postgres's default isolation level
Terminology: 'dead tuple' = a version no longer visible to any running or future transaction
Terminology: 'bloat' = space held by dead tuples and unused free space inside table and index pages

chapters.title: Tuple Headers: xmin, xmax, ctid
points: Every heap tuple carries a 23-byte HeapTupleHeader before its user data, padded to 24 bytes
t_xmin: the transaction ID that INSERTed this version
t_xmax: the transaction ID that DELETEd or UPDATEd this version; 0 means still live
t_cid: command ID, distinguishes statements inside one transaction so a statement doesn't see its own output
t_ctid: physical pointer (block number, offset) — points to itself for the newest version, or forward to the successor version after an UPDATE
System columns are queryable directly: SELECT xmin, xmax, ctid, * FROM t;
Inspect a row's lifecycle: UPDATE t SET v=v+1 WHERE id=1; then SELECT ctid,xmin,xmax FROM t WHERE id=1 shows a new ctid and a new xmin
t_infomask holds hint bits: HEAP_XMIN_COMMITTED, HEAP_XMIN_INVALID, HEAP_XMAX_COMMITTED, HEAP_XMAX_INVALID
Hint bits cache the commit-log answer in the tuple so later readers skip the clog lookup — this is why a pure SELECT can dirty pages
HEAP_XMIN_FROZEN (infomask bits combined) marks a tuple as visible to everyone, forever
xmax is overloaded: it also stores a MultiXactId when several transactions hold row locks on the same tuple (HEAP_XMAX_IS_MULTI)
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE / FOR SHARE sets xmax as a lock marker without deleting the row
Extension pageinspect exposes raw internals: SELECT * FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('t', 0));
Per-row overhead is real: 24-byte header + null bitmap + alignment padding on every version

chapters.title: Transaction IDs and the Commit Log
points: A transaction ID (xid) is a 32-bit unsigned counter, assigned lazily — read-only transactions get no real xid
txid_current() (modern name: pg_current_xact_id()) forces assignment of an xid and returns it
Special fixed xids: 0 = InvalidTransactionId, 1 = BootstrapXid, 2 = FrozenTransactionId
Real transaction ids begin at 3; comparisons use modulo-2^32 arithmetic, not plain integer comparison
Virtual transaction ids (backendID/localXID) let read-only work run without burning the global counter
The commit log (pg_xact, formerly pg_clog) stores 2 bits per transaction: IN_PROGRESS, COMMITTED, ABORTED, SUB_COMMITTED
Visibility checking = look at xmin/xmax, then ask pg_xact whether those transactions committed
Hint bits exist precisely to avoid repeating that pg_xact lookup on every read of the same tuple
Subtransactions (SAVEPOINT, PL/pgSQL EXCEPTION blocks) consume their own xids — a loop with EXCEPTION can burn ids fast
pg_subtrans maps a subtransaction to its parent so visibility resolves to the top-level commit state
An aborted transaction leaves its tuples on disk; they are simply never visible and become dead immediately
Because commit state is external, ROLLBACK costs O(1) regardless of how many rows were touched
COMMIT must flush WAL (unless synchronous_commit=off), which is why commit — not rollback — is the expensive side
Practical check: SELECT age(datfrozenxid) FROM pg_database; measures how far the counter has advanced past the oldest unfrozen xid

chapters.title: Snapshots and Visibility Rules
points: A snapshot captures: xmin (oldest still-running xid), xmax (next xid to be assigned), and xip_list (the in-progress list)
Visibility test, part 1: the tuple's xmin must be committed and must not be in the snapshot's in-progress set
Visibility test, part 2: the tuple's xmax must be 0, aborted, or still in progress — otherwise the version is gone
Rule of thumb: a tuple is visible if it was inserted before your snapshot and not deleted before your snapshot
Your own uncommitted changes are visible to you via command id (cid) comparison
READ COMMITTED takes a NEW snapshot at the start of each statement — two SELECTs in one transaction can differ
REPEATABLE READ takes ONE snapshot at the first statement and holds it for the whole transaction
SERIALIZABLE adds Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI): predicate locks detect dangerous read/write cycles and abort with SQLSTATE 40001
Under REPEATABLE READ, a conflicting UPDATE fails with 'could not serialize access due to concurrent update' — the app must retry
Under READ COMMITTED, an UPDATE that hits a concurrently-modified row does an EPQ re-check: it re-reads the newest version and re-tests the WHERE clause
That EPQ re-check is why READ COMMITTED can produce surprising results with UPDATE ... WHERE balance > 0 under concurrency
pg_export_snapshot() plus SET TRANSACTION SNAPSHOT lets pg_dump run parallel workers on one consistent view
Inspect live snapshot horizon: SELECT * FROM pg_snapshot_xmin(pg_current_snapshot());
Key insight: the OLDEST snapshot in the system pins every dead tuple newer than it — one idle transaction can block all cleanup

chapters.title: How INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE Actually Work
points: INSERT: write a new tuple with xmin = current xid, xmax = 0, ctid pointing to itself
DELETE: locate the tuple, set xmax = current xid; the bytes stay in the page
UPDATE = DELETE + INSERT: old version gets xmax = current xid, new version gets xmin = current xid
The old version's t_ctid is redirected to point at the new version, forming the update chain
Update chains let a concurrent writer walk forward to find the latest row version
Every UPDATE, even of a single boolean column, rewrites the ENTIRE row — Postgres has no partial row update
That means updating one column of a row with a 2 KB text field costs a full 2 KB rewrite
Consequence: every non-HOT UPDATE inserts a new entry into EVERY index on the table, even unmodified-column indexes
Write amplification example: a table with 6 indexes turns one UPDATE into 1 heap write + 6 index writes
TOAST: values over ~2 KB move to a side table; if the TOASTed column is unchanged, the new version reuses the same TOAST pointer
Table with only UPDATEs still grows — new versions need free space, and pages fill up
fillfactor (default 100 for tables) reserves space in each page for future versions; lowering to 80-90 helps update-heavy tables
ALTER TABLE t SET (fillfactor = 85); then VACUUM FULL t; to apply it to existing pages
Deleted rows are invisible immediately at commit, but the disk space returns only after VACUUM

chapters.title: HOT Updates and Page Pruning
points: HOT = Heap-Only Tuple: an optimization that avoids touching indexes on UPDATE
Two conditions for HOT: no INDEXED column changed, AND the new version fits on the SAME page as the old one
In a HOT update, the old tuple's line pointer becomes a redirect and the new tuple gets no index entry at all
Index scans land on the old item pointer and follow the HOT chain within the page to reach the live version
HOT chains never cross pages — that's why fillfactor matters so much for update-heavy tables
Benefit 1: no index write amplification; Benefit 2: HOT-pruning can reclaim space without a full VACUUM
Opportunistic pruning: any page access can trigger heap_page_prune, collapsing dead HOT chain members into free space
Pruning is cheap and local, but it cannot remove index entries — that still needs VACUUM
Measure it: SELECT relname, n_tup_upd, n_tup_hot_upd FROM pg_stat_user_tables; a high hot ratio is healthy
A hot_upd/n_tup_upd ratio near 0 on an update-heavy table means fillfactor is too high or an indexed column keeps changing
Classic anti-pattern: indexing a frequently-updated column (last_seen_at, status counter) kills HOT for the whole table
Postgres 16+ adds HOT support for updates when a summarizing (BRIN) index covers the changed column
Fix pattern: move the churning column into a separate narrow table with no indexes on it
Trade-off of low fillfactor: more pages for the same live rows, so sequential scans read more
PageIsFull hint bit tells later backends when a page is worth pruning

chapters.title: Dead Tuples, Bloat, and VACUUM
points: A tuple is dead when its xmax is committed and older than every active snapshot's xmin horizon
VACUUM does three jobs: mark dead tuple space reusable, remove matching index entries, and update the visibility map
Plain VACUUM does NOT return disk space to the OS — it only makes space reusable inside the file
Exception: VACUUM truncates the file if the trailing pages are entirely empty (and it can grab a brief ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock to do it)
VACUUM FULL rewrites the whole table into a new file, returning space to the OS, but takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock — it blocks all reads and writes
pg_repack and pg_squeeze do the same compaction online, without a long exclusive lock
The Free Space Map (fsm) records per-page free space so INSERTs can reuse vacuumed room
The Visibility Map (vm) has 2 bits per page: all-visible and all-frozen
all-visible pages enable INDEX ONLY SCANs — the executor skips the heap fetch entirely
Two-pass VACUUM: scan heap collecting dead tids, remove them from every index, then return to the heap and free the line pointers
maintenance_work_mem sizes the dead-tid array; too small means multiple index passes over the same table
Postgres 17 replaced that array with a TID store, cutting memory use and repeated index scans dramatically
Monitor bloat: SELECT relname, n_dead_tup, n_live_tup, last_autovacuum FROM pg_stat_user_tables ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC;
Diagnose a stuck vacuum: SELECT * FROM pg_stat_progress_vacuum;
Extension pgstattuple gives exact (expensive) bloat measurement: SELECT * FROM pgstattuple('big_table');

chapters.title: Autovacuum: Tuning the Cleanup Loop
points: The autovacuum launcher wakes every autovacuum_naptime (default 60s) and starts workers per database
autovacuum_max_workers (default 3) caps concurrent workers — a common bottleneck on servers with hundreds of tables
Vacuum threshold formula: autovacuum_vacuum_threshold (50) + autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor (0.2) × reltuples
0.2 scale factor means a 100M-row table waits for 20M dead tuples before vacuuming — far too late for big tables
Fix for large tables: ALTER TABLE big SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01, autovacuum_vacuum_threshold = 10000);
Postgres 13+ adds autovacuum_vacuum_insert_threshold so append-only tables get vacuumed for freezing and visibility map updates
ANALYZE has its own trigger: autovacuum_analyze_threshold + autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor (0.1) × reltuples
Cost-based delay throttles I/O: vacuum_cost_limit (200) of credits, then sleep autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay (2ms default in PG12+)
Cost accounting: vacuum_cost_page_hit=1, page_miss=2 (10 pre-PG14), page_dirty=20
On modern SSDs the default limit is far too conservative — raising vacuum_cost_limit to 1000-2000 is routine
Autovacuum yields to conflicting DDL: it cancels itself when a lock conflict appears — except in wraparound-prevention mode
Never set autovacuum = off; the outcome is unbounded bloat followed by a forced wraparound shutdown
Watch running workers: SELECT pid, query, backend_start FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE query LIKE 'autovacuum%';
log_autovacuum_min_duration = 0 logs every autovacuum run — the single most useful vacuum observability setting
Table-level overrides beat global tuning: set aggressive parameters only on the few hot tables that need them

chapters.title: Transaction ID Wraparound and Freezing
points: The xid counter is 32-bit: about 4.2 billion values, so 'past' and 'future' are decided by modulo-2^32 comparison
Any xid is visible-in-the-past for the ~2 billion values behind it and in-the-future for the ~2 billion ahead
If the counter laps a tuple's xmin, that row would suddenly appear to be from the future and VANISH — this is wraparound data loss
Freezing prevents it: mark a tuple's xmin as frozen so it is unconditionally visible regardless of the counter
Modern Postgres sets an infomask frozen bit instead of literally writing xid 2, preserving xmin for forensics
vacuum_freeze_min_age (50M): tuples older than this get frozen during a normal vacuum of a page
vacuum_freeze_table_age (150M): forces an aggressive scan that reads all-visible pages, not just the dirty ones
autovacuum_freeze_max_age (200M): triggers anti-wraparound autovacuum even if autovacuum is disabled
Anti-wraparound vacuum does NOT yield to lock conflicts — it is why a DDL-heavy table can suddenly block
At ~40M xids remaining Postgres logs warnings; at ~3M it refuses new write transactions and demands single-user mode VACUUM
Monitor constantly: SELECT datname, age(datfrozenxid) FROM pg_database ORDER BY 2 DESC;
Per-table view: SELECT relname, age(relfrozenxid) FROM pg_class WHERE relkind='r' ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 20;
MultiXactIds have a parallel 32-bit counter, pg_multixact, with its own autovacuum_multixact_freeze_max_age and its own wraparound risk
Blockers of freezing: long-running transactions, abandoned replication slots, unresolved prepared transactions, hot_standby_feedback
Postgres 14 added the failsafe: past vacuum_failsafe_age it drops cost delays and skips index cleanup to finish freezing fast
Postgres 18's asynchronous I/O and PG17's TID store both cut the wall-clock cost of the emergency freeze scan

chapters.title: Mistakes, Trade-offs, and the Whole Picture
points: Mistake 1: an idle-in-transaction connection holds a snapshot and blocks ALL cleanup database-wide — set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout
Mistake 2: an unused replication slot pins xmin forever; check pg_replication_slots and drop dead slots
Mistake 3: hot_standby_feedback = on lets a slow replica query hold back the primary's vacuum horizon
Mistake 4: a forgotten prepared transaction in pg_prepared_xacts freezes the horizon indefinitely
Find the culprit fast: SELECT pid, state, xact_start, now()-xact_start AS age FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state <> 'idle' ORDER BY xact_start;
Mistake 5: a queue table with high churn and no per-table autovacuum tuning — it bloats to 100x its live size
Mistake 6: reaching for VACUUM FULL on a production table during business hours; use pg_repack instead
Mistake 7: batch DELETEs of millions of rows with no follow-up VACUUM, leaving the file at peak size
Mistake 8: SELECT count(*) is slow because MVCC forces per-row visibility checks — no engine-level row count exists
Trade-off table row — Postgres in-heap versions: free rollback, no undo-log contention, but bloat and mandatory vacuum
Trade-off table row — InnoDB undo log: compact tables, but rollback cost scales with work and the undo log itself can grow
Trade-off table row — Oracle rollback segments: readers can fail with 'snapshot too old'; Postgres readers never do
Index-only scans are the payoff for keeping the visibility map fresh — vacuum is a performance feature, not just cleanup
Mental model to keep: xmin/xmax + snapshot = visibility; visibility horizon + time = dead tuples; dead tuples + no vacuum = bloat and wraparound
Daily health query set: n_dead_tup ratio, age(datfrozenxid), oldest xact_start, and last_autovacuum per hot table
